snippet.description:

E dopo i problemi al controllo aereo che nella notte tra venerdì e sabato hanno gettato nel caos i voli in tutti gli scali americani e quelli con destinazione Usa. Al momento, riferiscono i media, non c'è nessuna notizia di un possibile attacco informatico né di un collegamento con i recenti episodi di Microsoft e degli aerei.

snippet.title: Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, U.S. Bank customers can’t get their money. #banking #finance
snippet.description:
Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, U.S. Bank and Truist customers reported outages. People couldn’t log in, check their balances or send transfers. Chase said a technical issue was slowing transactions and that customers’ money was safe. No one has said what caused it yet.

Here’s the bigger problem: a regular savings account at a big bank pays as little as 0.01%. That’s $1 a year on $10,000.

High-yield savings accounts are paying way more right now:
SoFi: up to 4.40% APY (with direct deposit)
EverBank: 4.20% APY
Capital One 360 Performance Savings: about 3.2% APY

All three are FDIC insured. If the Fed raises rates in December, these rates could go even higher.

I’m a high school finance teacher, and this is one of the first things I teach my students: keep your emergency fund somewhere that actually pays you.

snippet.title: Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo outage: what we know #Shorts
snippet.description:
Chase, Bank of America and Wells Fargo customers reported trouble logging in, seeing balances and moving money on Monday, with U.S. Bank, Capital One, Truist and Zelle users reporting problems too. Chase says a technical issue is slowing some transactions but customers still have access to their accounts and funds. Wells Fargo says online banking is temporarily unavailable; ATMs, branches and phone bankers still work. Bank of America declined to comment. No bank has announced a cause or said service is restored.
Scammers exploit outages: never give a password or one-time code to anyone who calls or texts claiming to be support. Check your bank's official app, website or X support account.

snippet.title: Bank of America Fined $1.2 Billion
snippet.description:
Bank of America’s $1.2 Billion Fine: What Went Wrong With Risk Management?

Bank of America is facing billions of dollars in penalties and settlements related to failures in financial crime compliance, including anti-money laundering (AML), the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA), and sanctions violations. In this video, I break down the regulatory actions involving FinCEN, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), and the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), and explain why this case deserves more attention from the risk management and quantitative finance communities.

But beyond the headlines and dollar amounts, there is a much bigger story: What happens when the models, controls, processes, and governance frameworks designed to prevent financial crime don't deliver the expected results?

From a quantitative risk management perspective, we explore several important areas:

snippet.description:
Bank of America's $550 metal card just arrived — and the rule that made this card famous quietly changed this year.
In this first look: the unboxing, the $550 fee and 75,000-point welcome offer (after $5,000 spend in 90 days — $750 as cash, ~$938 toward airfare), 2x on travel and dining and 1.5x on everything else, and the credits math — $300/year airline incidental credit, $150/year lifestyle credit, and the $120 Global Entry / TSA PreCheck credit.
Then the party tricks: four Priority Pass memberships on one account, still including Priority Pass restaurants, and the double boost — your BofA Rewards tier multiplies what you earn, and flights booked with points through BofA Travel cost 20% fewer points.
The twist: in May 2026, BofA Rewards replaced Preferred Rewards. The 75% earn boost now needs $1M in BofA/Merrill balances (Premier tier); $100K now gets 50% — 3x on travel and dining, 2.25x on everything else. Older members are grandfathered at 75% for a while, so check which tier you're actually on.
The catch: no airline or hotel transfer partners — points are fixed-value, so 1.25¢ toward airfare is the ceiling.
Verdict: worth it if you bank with BofA/Merrill and will use the credits anyway; skip it if you want transfer partners.

snippet.title: Bank Of America Hit With A SEVERE SENTENCE — CEO Says “I’m Not Concerned”!
snippet.description:
🚨 A quick clarification: Bank of America’s punishment involves financial penalties and regulatory enforcement—not a criminal prison sentence against its CEO. Treasury announced more than $1.21 billion in penalties over anti-money laundering and sanctions violations. The $5 billion figure refers to suspicious transactions that were not reported on time, not money conclusively proven to be criminal proceeds.

🔴 WHAT DID BANK OF AMERICA DO WRONG?

Bank of America admitted to willfully violating the Bank Secrecy Act. Regulators identified failures in its anti-money laundering program, customer due diligence and suspicious activity reporting. The OCC says serious problems continued after a December 2024 order required the bank to address its compliance weaknesses. How did a bank with such extensive resources allow those failures to persist?

💬 WHAT DID THE CEO MEAN BY “I’M NOT CONCERNED”?

During his CNBC interview, Brian Moynihan said “I’m not concerned” when asked about Bank of America’s standing with the Trump administration. That context matters: he was answering a question about the bank’s relationship with Washington. Elsewhere in the interview, he described additional staffing and ongoing efforts to fix the compliance problems.

⚖️ DOES A BILLION-DOLLAR PENALTY DELIVER ACCOUNTABILITY?

The OCC assessed a $750 million penalty that is credited toward FinCEN’s $1.2 billion fine—not added on top of it. The enforcement actions also require further corrective work. This raises a larger question: can financial penalties change a major bank’s behavior if earlier regulatory orders failed to resolve serious weaknesses?

🏦 TWO CONTROVERSIES, ONE QUESTION ABOUT TRUST.

This video also examines the separate debate over debanking, Trump’s public criticism of major banks and the concerns raised by customers who say they were denied financial services. We distinguish those allegations from the bank’s admitted compliance violations—and examine what meaningful accountability should look like for executives, shareholders and customers.

🎥 We break down the penalties, the $5 billion in suspicious activity, Moynihan’s response and the unresolved questions about oversight at one of America’s largest banks.

👉 Subscribe for more on U.S. politics, corporate accountability and the decisions affecting your financial future.

💬 Should bank executives face personal financial consequences when serious compliance failures continue—or are billion-dollar penalties enough to force change?

The card survived. In 1976, it got a new name: Visa.
